abstract: >-
  Simulation-based cutoff values for conditional item fit can be estimated by
  parametric bootstrapping and reported as an interval of a chosen width.
  Johansson (2025) recommended this over rule-of-thumb critical values but gave
  iteration guidance without accounting for the error rate that the interval
  width controls. This paper re-examines iterations and width against the
  familywise error rate (FWER), and compares FWER and false discovery rate
  control, in seven simulation studies with dichotomous and polytomous items.
  The interval width is shown to set the FWER of the interval rule jointly with
  the number of items. Bootstrap p-values with a Westfall-Young step-down target
  that error rate directly and detect more misfit than a width-matched interval.
  When all items fit, their FWER was at or slightly below the nominal level from
  400 iterations, and the small excess at fewer iterations came from how the
  statistics are studentized. Holm performed similarly once iterations cleared
  its floor, which grows with the number of items, while Benjamini-Hochberg
  flagged more fitting items. When some items misfit, every procedure exceeded
  its nominal rate at large samples, because misfit contaminates the total score
  that conditional fit is computed on. Conditional outfit was less powerful than
  infit throughout. Recommendations include flagging items on the Westfall-Young
  corrected p-value, using at least 400 iterations and 1000 to 2000 for a final
  analysis, reporting the interval as a descriptive band at width .95, and
  removing items one at a time. The methods are available in the R package
  `easyRasch2` and the jamovi module `easyRasch2jmv`.

# Introduction

Psychometric analysis often relies on rule-of-thumb critical values for interpreting fit metrics, but no fixed value or range can generalize across analyses, because the distribution of a fit statistic under a correctly fitting model depends on features of the data and the model, such as the sample size and the number of items [@muller_item_2020;@mcneish_direct_2024]. Simulation-based critical values for Rasch infit and outfit, obtained by parametric bootstrap, were proposed by Wolfe [-@wolfe_computer_2008; -@wolfe_bootstrap_2013] and examined across sample sizes and test lengths by Seol [-@seol_using_2016]. Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025] applied this approach to conditional item infit [@muller_item_2020] and evaluated it through a series of simulation studies using the `easyRasch` R package [@easyrasch2024]. Infit with simulation-based cutoffs outperformed the item-restscore method [@kreiner_note_2011] with samples below 500 respondents, and the paper provided practical guidance on sample sizes, iterative item removal, and the number of bootstrap iterations. The present paper builds on that work and corrects parts of it.

The iteration guidance in Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025] recommended 100 bootstrap iterations for samples up to 250 respondents and 200 to 400 iterations for larger samples. That guidance was based on detection rates, since fewer iterations appeared to detect more misfit items with smaller samples. This paper shows that the apparent advantage was an artifact. With few iterations the cutoff interval is estimated from too little information, becomes narrower than its nominal width, and flags fitting items at an inflated rate. Detection was in effect bought with false positives. The false positive rates reported in the earlier paper were calculated per item, while the probability of at least one false flag across all items in a scale, the familywise error rate (FWER), was not examined. 

Three contributions follow. First, the interval width and the number of iterations must be chosen jointly. The width sets the FWER of the interval decision rule, and the number of iterations determines whether the nominal width is attained at all. Second, the same bootstrap supports p-values with multiplicity corrections. The Westfall-Young (WY) step-down [@westfall_resampling_1993] targets the FWER directly and controls it when all items fit, detects more misfit than the interval rule at matched error rates, and needs far fewer iterations than the interval rule or the Holm procedure. The Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure [@benjamini_controlling_1995], which controls the false discovery rate instead, is included for comparison and comes with an iteration floor that grows with the number of comparisons. Third, the paper introduces decision stability as an outcome in its own right: whether re-running the same analysis on the same data with a different random seed produces the same set of flagged items.

Results are presented using two simple performance metrics, detection rate and false positive rate, with decision stability added as a third. Readers interested in the statistical foundations of the multiple testing methods are referred to Westfall and Young [-@westfall_resampling_1993] and to the more recent paper by Ferreira [-@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024]. All analyses use conditional item fit as implemented in the `iarm` R package [@mueller_iarm_2022], accessed through `easyRasch2` [@johanssonEasyRasch2PsychometricAnalysis2026]. The bootstrap is parametric throughout. Datasets are simulated from the Rasch model fitted to the observed data, and the model is refitted to every simulated dataset, so the item parameters are re-estimated in each bootstrap sample. The reasons to avoid unconditional item fit statistics, which is implemented in most other software, are detailed in Müller [-@muller_item_2020].

The paper proceeds as follows. The next two sections describe the cutoff interval and the decision rules based on bootstrap p-values. The Method section describes the simulation design. Three results sections then cover interval convergence and error rates, the comparison between interval-based and p-value-based decisions, and decision stability. The Discussion summarizes the findings as practical recommendations.

# The interval and its width

The procedure under study uses a parametric bootstrap to establish critical values for conditional item infit [@muller_item_2020]. Item thresholds are estimated from the observed data by conditional maximum likelihood, and person locations by weighted likelihood [@warm_weighted_1989]. Each of $B$ simulated datasets draws $n$ person locations with replacement from the estimated ones and generates responses under the Rasch model, or the partial credit model for polytomous items [@masters_rasch_1982], with the estimated thresholds, so every simulated dataset fits the model by construction. The model is refitted to each simulated dataset by conditional maximum likelihood, so the item parameters are re-estimated in every bootstrap sample as in the analysis of the observed data, and conditional infit is computed from that refit. This yields an empirical null distribution of $B$ values per item. Each item's null distribution is summarized by a highest density interval of width $w$, and an observed infit value outside the interval flags the item as misfitting.

The endpoints of the interval are extreme order statistics of the $B$ simulated values, and how well they can be estimated depends on the expected number of simulated values beyond each endpoint, about $(1 - w)B/2$, here called draws per tail. With $B$ = 400, for example, that number is 10 at $w$ = .95 but 0.2 at $w$ = .999 (@tbl-drawspertail gives it for other combinations). With fewer than one draw per tail, the interval equals the range of the simulated values, its nominal width is not attained, and its realized width keeps growing as $B$ increases. The number of iterations an interval needs therefore depends on $w$, and not on the sample size that the iteration guidance in Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025] was conditioned on.

Once the interval has reached its nominal width, a fitting item is flagged with probability $1 - w$. With $k$ items tested jointly, and treating the item statistics as independent, the probability that at least one fitting item is flagged is

$$
\text{FWER} = 1 - w^k,
$$ {#eq-fwer}

the FWER of the interval rule [@sidak_rectangular_1967]. The width is thus the error rate parameter of the decision rule rather than a display choice. For a 20-item scale, $w$ = .999 gives a FWER of 2.0% and $w$ = .99 gives 18.2%. Item fit statistics are positively dependent through the shared total score, which makes @eq-fwer a slightly conservative upper bound, and the simulation studies below confirm it across item counts and item formats.

# Bootstrap p-values and multiplicity corrections

The same $B$ simulated values support a different decision rule. Let $F_i$ denote the observed infit of item $i$ and $F^*_{ib}$ the simulated values. Each is studentized by the simulation mean and standard deviation, $t_i = (F_i - \bar{F}^*_i)/s^*_i$, which puts items with different locations on a common scale, since the expected infit range varies with item location relative to the sample [@muller_item_2020]. This follows Ferreira [-@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024, Section 4], who standardizes each statistic by its null mean and variance so that the maximum across comparisons treats them equally. In his permutation setting those moments are known and shared by the observed and permuted statistics, while here they are estimated from the simulated values. The marginal Monte Carlo p-value is

$$
p_i = \frac{1 + \sum_{b=1}^{B} I\left(|t^*_{ib}| \geq |t_i|\right)}{B + 1},
$$ {#eq-pmarg}

where $I(\cdot)$ equals 1 when its argument is true and 0 otherwise.

Its smallest attainable value is $1/(B+1)$, which sets the resolution of the test. When the observed statistic and the simulated ones are exchangeable under the null, as the observed and permuted statistics of a permutation test are, a p-value of this form is valid at any $B$ [@dufour_monte_2006, Proposition 2.2]. Two features of the procedure prevent that here.

First, the null hypothesis is composite, since the simulated datasets are drawn from the model fitted to the observed data rather than from the model that generated them. Dufour [-@dufour_monte_2006, Section 6] calls such a test, with the nuisance parameters replaced by a point estimate, a local Monte Carlo test, valid asymptotically under regularity conditions rather than at a given sample size. The procedure thus belongs to the bootstrap methods that Ferreira [-@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024, Section 5] describes as controlling error rates approximately, with an accuracy at finite sample sizes that has to be checked rather than assumed. Second, the observed statistic is studentized by moments it did not contribute to (mean and standard deviation), while each simulated statistic is studentized by moments that include it, so the test is slightly liberal, by an amount that shrinks as $1/B$. Studentizing all $B + 1$ values by moments computed over the observed and simulated values together removes this asymmetry. This joint studentization is the Monte Carlo counterpart of Ferreira's shared moments, and the error-rate study evaluates both versions on the same simulated values.

Either way, the marginal p-value controls the error rate of a single pre-specified comparison. Scanning all $k$ items inflates the familywise error toward the levels in @eq-fwer, which is the argument for correcting it, not for abandoning p-values.

The WY step-down corrects for multiplicity using the joint distribution that the bootstrap already provides [@westfall_resampling_1993; @ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024]. The most extreme observed statistic is compared against the distribution of the maximum across all items,

$$
\tilde{p}_{(1)} = \frac{1 + \sum_{b=1}^{B} I\left(\max_i |t^*_{ib}| \geq |t_{(1)}|\right)}{B + 1},
$$ {#eq-wy}

after which the maximum is recomputed over the remaining items for the next statistic, with monotonicity enforced. Only $B \geq 1/\alpha$ iterations, that is 20 at $\alpha = .05$, are needed for a rejection to be possible at all. Ferreira [-@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024, Section 3] derives the step-down as a shortcut to the closure principle under the subset pivotality condition of Westfall and Young [-@westfall_resampling_1993]: the joint distribution of the statistics of any set of true hypotheses must not depend on whether the remaining hypotheses are true. The bootstrap reference distribution is that of the complete null by construction, but Ferreira's Example 2, tests of pairwise correlations computed from the same variables, shows that the condition fails when statistics share data, and every conditional fit statistic shares the total score it is conditioned on. The step-down can therefore be expected to control the FWER when all items fit, which is weak control, but not necessarily when some items misfit.

The BH procedure [@benjamini_controlling_1995] instead controls the false discovery rate, the expected proportion of flagged items that are in fact fitting. When a single item stands out, its adjusted p-value is bounded below by $m/(B+1)$ for $m$ comparisons, so it cannot be flagged unless

$$
B \geq \frac{m}{\alpha}.
$$ {#eq-bhfloor}

When $s$ comparisons have p-values at the Monte Carlo floor of @eq-pmarg, the smallest attainable adjusted p-value is $m/(s(B+1))$, so several clearly misfitting items lower the required $B$. With 20 items and $\alpha = .05$, a single misfitting item cannot be flagged unless $B \geq 400$.

The Holm procedure [@holm_simple_1979] is the familiar FWER alternative based on the marginal p-values alone. It controls the FWER under general conditions, needs no pivotality condition, and little improvement on it is possible among procedures that use only the marginal p-values [@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024, Section 2]. Procedures that use the joint distribution, such as the step-down, can be more powerful when the statistics are dependent, but the gain is small when they are close to independent, as the agreement with @eq-fwer reported below suggests item fit statistics are. Holm shares the reachability floor of @eq-bhfloor, which for Holm is not lowered when several items stand out. Ferreira [-@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024] gives a self-contained account of these methods for 5 to 50 hypotheses, the range of item-level analysis.

All of these rules are computed from one bootstrap and inherit its approximate validity, and the simulation studies quantify how close each comes to its nominal error rate.

# Method

```{r method-prep}
#| include: false
real_fit <- s_cal$real_fit
rf <- setNames(sprintf("%.2f", real_fit$Infit_MSQ), real_fit$Item)
anch <- aggregate(infit ~ rho, data = s_cal$anchor, FUN = mean)
anch <- anch[order(anch$rho), ]
av <- sprintf("%.2f", anch$infit)   # rho .75, .85, .90
# five-item calibration (calibration_rho_short.R), pooled over n
m5 <- function(r) mean(s_cal5$grid$infit[abs(s_cal5$grid$rho - r) < 1e-9], na.rm = TRUE)
# twenty-item polytomous scan and the nine-item phq9 anchor, both at the same rho
p20 <- function(r) mean(s_cal$grid$infit[abs(s_cal$grid$rho - r) < 1e-9 &
                                         s_cal$grid$format == "polytomous"], na.rm = TRUE)
ph85 <- function() mean(s_cal$anchor$infit[abs(s_cal$anchor$rho - 0.85) < 1e-9], na.rm = TRUE)
# descriptives of the phq9 data behind the real item set
ph_obs <- load_phq9_arm()$obs
ph_tot <- rowSums(ph_obs)
ph_zero <- sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(ph_tot == 0))
ph_med <- sprintf("%.0f", median(ph_tot))
ph_max <- 3 * ncol(ph_obs)
ph_z <- function(it) sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(ph_obs[, it] == 0))
```

## Overview

Seven simulation studies were conducted, and @tbl-studies summarizes their designs. Each answers one question, and its design follows from that question.

The first two use the 20 dichotomous items of Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025], so that the iteration guidance of that paper is re-examined on the item set it was derived from. The first asks how many iterations the cutoff interval needs at a given width. Convergence concerns the null distribution alone, so it uses null data only, run to $B$ = 10 000 as a reference. The second asks what error rates the decision rules have across widths and iteration counts, with misfit at $\rho$ = .15, the strong misfit of the earlier paper. The third compares the rules on polytomous items at a misfit severity anchored on a real dataset, as described below, so that they are compared at a severity analysts observe rather than one chosen to be detectable. It uses PHQ-9 item parameters for a real configuration and a stylised 15-item set for a regular one. The fourth holds datasets fixed and varies only the bootstrap seed, because decision stability concerns one dataset analyzed twice. It spans misfit from strong to anchored, since stability depends on how many items lie near the decision threshold. The fifth replaces multidimensionality with random responding at matched infit, to check whether two findings belong to the misfit mechanism rather than to misfit in general. The sixth applies the recommended rule and number of iterations to conditional outfit, the second statistic the same bootstrap produces. The seventh repeats the error-rate and rule comparisons on a five-item scale, where @eq-fwer predicts the lowest error rates and the reachability floor of BH no longer binds.

Within each replication, the five interval widths ($w$ = .90, .95, .99, .995, and .999) and the decision rules are computed from the same bootstrap, so comparisons between widths and between rules are paired, and in the sixth study so is the comparison between infit and outfit. In the two dichotomous studies every smaller $B$ is evaluated on the first $B$ draws of a single bootstrap per replication, so comparisons between values of $B$ are paired as well, and the two studies share their null replications. Replication counts differ because the studies estimate different quantities with different precision, and the Monte Carlo error of each is reported in @tbl-mcse.

| Study | Items | $\rho$ | Misfitting items | $n$ | $B$ | Replications |
|:-------------------|:-------------------|:------------|:-----------|:----------|:------------|:--------------|
| Interval convergence | 20 dichotomous | none | 0 | 150 to 1000 | 100 to 10 000 | 500 |
| Error rates over $(w, B)$ | 20 dichotomous | .15 | 0, 1, 3 | 150 to 1000 | 100 to 10 000 | 500 / 250 |
| PHQ-9-anchored misfit | 15 polytomous, 9 phq9 | .75, .85, .90 | 0 to 3 | 150 to 1000 | 100, 400, 2000 | 120 |
| Decision stability | 15 polytomous, 9 phq9 | .15, .50, .85 | 0 or all | 250, 1000 | 100 to 2000 | 10 datasets x 25 seeds |
| Mechanism check | 9 phq9 | random responses | 1, 2 | 250, 1000 | 100, 400, 2000 | 120 |
| Infit versus outfit | 20 dichotomous, 9 phq9 | .60, .85 | 0, 1 | 250, 600 | 1000 | 250 |
| Short scale | 5 polytomous | .75 | 0, 1 | 250, 600 | 100, 400, 2000 | 1000 / 250 |

: Overview of the simulation studies {#tbl-studies}

*Note.* Misfitting item counts are 1 and 3 for the 20-item and 15-item sets and 1 and 2 for the 9-item set, with 0 denoting the null condition used for error rates. The $n$ = 150 condition is included for the 9-item set only. In the sixth study the two correlations belong to the two item sets in the order listed, chosen so that both inject comparable infit, and its single misfitting item is run as two separate conditions, once near the person mean and once off target. The null replications shared by the first two studies number 500 per sample size. The misfit conditions of the second study run to $B$ = 2000 with 250 replications each. The seventh study uses 1000 replications for its null conditions, which carry the error-rate claim, and 250 for its misfit conditions.

## Data generation

Misfit is induced by multidimensionality, as in Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025], in every study but the mechanism check. Fitting items are generated from a primary latent dimension and misfitting items from a second dimension, with person locations drawn from a bivariate normal distribution where $\rho$ denotes the correlation between the two dimensions. Lower values of $\rho$ produce stronger misfit. The null conditions, with no misfitting items, use a single dimension.

The mechanism check replaces multidimensionality with random responding, in which a fixed proportion of the responses to the target items is replaced by a uniform draw over the response categories. That proportion was set so that a single target item has the same expected infit as in the multidimensional condition, which puts the two mechanisms on equal footing at matched misfit severity.

The dichotomous item set replicates the design of the earlier paper: 20 items with locations drawn uniformly between -2 and 2 logits, person locations with a standard deviation of 1.5, and response data generated with the `eRm` package [@mair_extended_2007]. Misfitting items are those located nearest 0, -1, and -2 logits relative to the person mean, so that targeting varies. Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025] drew every sample from one master dataset of 10 000 simulated respondents per condition. Here every replication of every study generates its respondents anew, so replications are independent and no chance feature of one master dataset is shared by all the replications of a condition. The sixth study reuses this item set and contrasts two single-item conditions, one misfitting the item nearest the person mean at 0.04 logits and one misfitting the most off-target item at 1.82 logits. This mirrors the q5 and q8 contrast in the PHQ-9 set (see below).

The polytomous item sets use four ordered response categories. The stylised set has 15 items with locations evenly spaced between -2 and 2 logits and item thresholds spread one logit around each location, again with person standard deviation 1.5. The second set takes its item parameters from the phq9 dataset included in `easyRasch2`, nine depression screening items with four response categories answered by 600 respondents. The data are a subsample of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey [@cdc_nhanes_2024] in which respondents with all-zero responses were randomly thinned, to avoid the zero-inflated response pattern of the full survey data. In the resulting data `r ph_zero`% of respondents have a total score of 0 and the median total score is `r ph_med` of `r ph_max`, so the sample leans toward the upper half of the scale. Zero responses are concentrated in two items, q8 (`r ph_z(8)`%) and q9 (`r ph_z(9)`%), the items located furthest above the person mean. The configuration is therefore unusual in having two off-target items rather than in having a floor effect, and the stylised 15-item set provides a regular configuration for comparison. Thresholds were estimated with conditional maximum likelihood and the latent standard deviation of 1.39 was estimated from the same data. This set represents the item properties of a real instrument rather than stylised ones. Its misfitting items were designated to be q5, located near the person mean, and q8, the most off-target item at 1.4 logits above the mean, so that targeting again varies.

## Calibrating misfit severity

Misfit severity is reported and calibrated on the infit scale rather than on $\rho$, for two reasons. First, the same $\rho$ produces very different infit depending on item format. @tbl-calibration shows that at identical item locations and person distributions, polytomous items yield roughly 2.8 times the infit excess of dichotomous items, because more response categories carry more information per item. The $\rho$ = .15 used in the earlier paper was chosen to represent a clearly misfitting dichotomous item. Carried unchanged into polytomous items it would produce infit values beyond what real data show. Second, infit is the scale on which analysts observe misfit, so calibrating on it connects the simulation conditions to practice.

The same non-portability holds across item counts. A separate scan on the five-item set used in the short-scale study gives a mean injected infit of `r sprintf("%.2f", m5(0.85))` at $\rho$ = .85, against `r sprintf('%.2f', p20(0.85))` for the same $\rho$ on the twenty-item polytomous set built to the same recipe, with the nine phq9 items falling between at `r sprintf('%.2f', ph85())`. Reaching the anchored range at five items requires $\rho$ = .75, which gives `r sprintf("%.2f", m5(0.75))`. A short scale needs stronger misfit to show the same infit, because the misfitting item is a larger share of the total score that the statistic is conditioned on and therefore attenuates its own value more. Anchoring on infit rather than on $\rho$ keeps the conditions comparable across item counts as well as formats.  We remind readers that infit is strongly dependent on sample size [@muller_item_2020] and traditional rule-of-thumb thresholds should be avoided when interpreting infit values.

```{r tbl-calibration}
#| tbl-cap: "Conditional infit by item format and inter-dimensional correlation"
cal <- s_cal$grid |>
  summarise(infit = mean(infit, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(rho, format)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = format, values_from = infit) |>
  arrange(rho) |>
  mutate(ratio = (polytomous - 1) / (dichotomous - 1))
knitr::kable(cal, digits = 2,
             col.names = c("Correlation", "Dichotomous", "Polytomous",
                           "Excess ratio"))
```

*Note.* Mean conditional infit of a single misfitting item under identical conditions (20 items, identical locations, $n$ = 500, 60 replications). The excess ratio is the polytomous infit excess over 1.0 divided by the dichotomous excess.

The misfit level used for the rule comparisons, referred to below as the PHQ-9-anchored or anchored level, is set against the phq9 dataset with $n$ = 600. Analyzing the observed responses with simulation-based cutoffs ($B$ = 1000) and WY corrected p-values flags three underfitting items, q3 at `r rf["q3"]`, q8 at `r rf["q8"]`, and q9 at `r rf["q9"]`, along with two overfitting items at `r rf["q2"]` and `r rf["q4"]`. A calibration scan on the phq9 item parameters shows that $\rho$ = .85 and .90 together reproduce this range, with mean infit values of `r av[2]` and `r av[3]` for a single misfitting item, close to the strongest and the mildest flagged real items. The level .75 gives `r av[1]`, slightly beyond the worst real item. The stability study additionally includes $\rho$ = .15 and .50 to span the range from the strong misfit used in the earlier paper down to the anchored level.

Matching mean conditional infit places a misfitting item at the same observed severity on the statistic that analysts see, which is why it was chosen. It does not equate the alternative distributions, the contamination of the conditioning score or the difficulty of detection, and the mechanism check reported below shows that conditions with the same mean infit can produce very different false positive rates. The anchored level is therefore one empirically observed severity, under multidimensionality, and not a representative sample of the misfit that analysts encounter.

## Decision rules and performance metrics

Four decision rules are compared, each computed from the same bootstrap as the others wherever more than one is evaluated. The interval rule flags an item when its observed infit falls outside the highest density interval, evaluated at each of the five widths. The three p-value rules flag an item when its marginal, WY corrected, or BH corrected p-value falls below $\alpha$ = .05, as described in the previous section. Holm, computed from the same marginal p-values, is reported alongside them as a second FWER procedure.

Three performance metrics are reported. The detection rate is the percentage of misfitting items that are flagged. The false positive rate is the percentage of fitting items that are flagged. The familywise false positive rate is the percentage of replications in which at least one fitting item is flagged, which under the null conditions estimates the familywise error rate that @eq-fwer describes. The stability metrics are defined in their own section below.

## Software and execution

All simulations were run in R 4.6.1 [@r2026] using `easyRasch2` [@johanssonEasyRasch2PsychometricAnalysis2026], which estimates item parameters with conditional maximum likelihood. Results were produced under `easyRasch2` versions 1.1.0 and 1.1.1, and the two dichotomous studies under version 1.4.0. The versions are identical in everything the simulations use, apart from the `statistic` argument added in 1.1.1 that the infit-versus-outfit study requires. In the polytomous studies every combination of replication and iteration count uses an independent bootstrap. In the two dichotomous studies the values of $B$ are nested within one bootstrap per replication, as described above. The code, the cached results, and the computational setup are described in the online supplement.

# Interval convergence and error rates

```{r r4-prep}
#| include: false
# --- convergence study -------------------------------------------------------
CV <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(s_conv$grid)), function(i) {
  r <- s_conv$res[[i]]
  if (is.null(r)) return(NULL)
  cbind(rep = s_conv$grid$rep[i], n = s_conv$grid$n[i], r)
}))
relw <- CV |>
  summarise(v = median(width), .by = c(n, w, B)) |>
  mutate(rel = v / v[B == max(B)], .by = c(n, w))

# largest discrepancy between sample sizes, over all (w, B)
n_spread <- relw |>
  summarise(sp = max(rel) - min(rel), .by = c(w, B)) |>
  summarise(mx = max(sp)) |> pull(mx)

# smallest B reaching 99 percent of the converged width
b99 <- relw |>
  summarise(m = median(rel), .by = c(w, B)) |>
  summarise(B99 = min(B[m >= 0.99]), .by = w) |> arrange(w)
bq <- function(wv) fmt_n(b99$B99[abs(b99$w - wv) < 1e-9])

rwn <- function(wv, Bv) median(
  relw$rel[abs(relw$w - wv) < 1e-9 & relw$B == Bv])
rw <- function(wv, Bv) sprintf("%.2f", rwn(wv, Bv))
# percent by which the interval falls short of its converged width
short <- function(wv, Bv, dp = 0) sprintf(paste0("%.", dp, "f"),
                                          100 * (1 - rwn(wv, Bv)))

# --- five-item short scale: BH vs WY, paired within replication --------------
P7 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(s_short$grid)), function(i) {
  r <- s_short$res[[i]]$pval
  if (is.null(r)) return(NULL)
  g <- s_short$grid[i, c("k", "n", "rep"), drop = FALSE]
  rownames(g) <- NULL
  cbind(g, r)
})) |>
  mutate(is_mis = k > 0 & item == s_short$mis)
rules5 <- P7 |>
  filter(k > 0, B == 2000) |>
  summarise(det_wy = 100 * mean(padj_fwer[is_mis] < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
            det_bh = 100 * mean(padj_bh[is_mis] < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
            fp_wy  = 100 * mean(padj_fwer[!is_mis] < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
            fp_bh  = 100 * mean(padj_bh[!is_mis] < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
            .by = n)
# named bh5 to avoid clashing with the r5 data frame in the section 5 prep chunk
bh5 <- function(nn, f) sprintf("%.1f", rules5[[f]][rules5$n == nn])

# --- five-item short scale (study 7): familywise rates under the null ---------
S7 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(s_short$grid)), function(i) {
  r <- s_short$res[[i]]$hdci
  if (is.null(r)) return(NULL)
  g <- s_short$grid[i, c("k", "n", "rep"), drop = FALSE]
  rownames(g) <- NULL
  cbind(g, r)
}))
fwe5 <- S7 |>
  filter(k == 0, B == 2000) |>
  summarise(any = as.integer(sum(code > 0) > 0), .by = c(w, n, rep)) |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(any), R = n(), .by = c(w, n)) |>
  mutate(pred = 100 * (1 - w^5),
         se = 100 * sqrt((pct / 100) * (1 - pct / 100) / R),
         z = (pct - pred) / se) |>
  arrange(n, w)
maxz5 <- max(abs(fwe5$z))
reps5 <- max(fwe5$R)
# bootstraps that produced no usable p-value at all
drop5 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(s_short$grid)), function(i) {
  r <- s_short$res[[i]]$pval
  if (is.null(r)) return(NULL)
  g <- s_short$grid[i, c("k", "n", "rep"), drop = FALSE]
  rownames(g) <- NULL
  cbind(g, r)
})) |>
  summarise(bad = all(is.na(p_marg)), .by = c(k, n, B, rep)) |>
  filter(n == 250) |>
  summarise(n_bad = sum(bad), n_all = n()) 
# the five widths in ascending order, as a readable inline list
s5 <- function(nn) {
  v <- fwe5$pct[fwe5$n == nn][order(fwe5$w[fwe5$n == nn])]
  paste0(paste(sprintf("%.1f", v[-length(v)]), collapse = ", "),
         " and ", sprintf("%.1f", v[length(v)]), "%")
}

# --- familywise error under the null, all three item sets --------------------
G0 <- bind_part(s_grid, "hdci", c("rep", "k", "n")) |>
  filter(k == 0) |> mutate(items = 20L, arm = "20 dichotomous")
P0 <- bind_part(s_poly, "hdci", c("arm", "rep", "k", "n", "rho")) |>
  filter(k == 0) |>
  mutate(items = ifelse(arm == "sim15", 15L, 9L),
         arm = ifelse(arm == "sim15", "15 polytomous", "9 phq9"))
NUL <- bind_rows(G0 |> select(arm, items, rep, n, B, w, item, code),
                 P0 |> select(arm, items, rep, n, B, w, item, code))
fwe <- NUL |>
  summarise(any = any(code > 0), .by = c(arm, items, w, B, n, rep)) |>
  summarise(obs = 100 * mean(any), .by = c(arm, items, w, B)) |>
  mutate(pred = 100 * (1 - w^items))
fq <- function(arm_, wv, Bv) sprintf("%.1f", fwe$obs[
  fwe$arm == arm_ & abs(fwe$w - wv) < 1e-9 & fwe$B == Bv])
pq <- function(arm_, wv) sprintf("%.1f", unique(fwe$pred[
  fwe$arm == arm_ & abs(fwe$w - wv) < 1e-9]))

# agreement with the Sidak prediction for the widths converged at B = 2000
conv_ok <- fwe |> filter(B == 2000, w <= 0.99) |> mutate(ratio = obs / pred)

# --- the artifact: detection and false positives at w = .999 -----------------
ART <- bind_part(s_grid, "hdci", c("rep", "k", "n")) |>
  filter(k == 3, abs(w - 0.999) < 1e-9) |>
  mutate(is_mis = item %in% s_grid$misfit) |>
  summarise(det = 100 * mean(code[is_mis] > 0),
            fp = 100 * mean(code[!is_mis] > 0), .by = c(n, B)) |>
  arrange(n, B)
aq <- function(n_, col, dp = 0) paste(sprintf(paste0("%.", dp, "f"),
                                              ART[[col]][ART$n == n_]),
                                      collapse = ", ")
fw999 <- fwe |> filter(arm == "20 dichotomous", abs(w - 0.999) < 1e-9)

# single misfitting item, same item set: detection is at ceiling throughout
k1det <- bind_part(s_grid, "hdci", c("rep", "k", "n")) |>
  filter(k == 1, abs(w - 0.999) < 1e-9, n == 150,
         item == s_grid$misfit[1]) |>
  summarise(det = 100 * mean(code > 0), .by = B)
```

This section reports the two studies that use dichotomous items, together with the null conditions of the polytomous studies. The first question is how many iterations the cutoff interval needs before it attains its nominal width. The second is what the error rate of the interval rule then is, and whether @eq-fwer describes it.

## How many iterations the interval needs

@fig-convergence shows the median interval width at each number of iterations, expressed relative to the width obtained from all 10 000 iterations of the same bootstrap, the reference width. Two results follow. First, the required number of iterations depends on the width and not on the sample size. Lines for the same width overlap almost exactly across the four sample sizes, with a largest discrepancy of `r sprintf("%.3f", n_spread)` at any combination of width and iterations. Convergence is a property of the simulated null distribution and its tails, and the sample size affects where that distribution sits rather than how many values are needed to describe its extremes.

```{r fig-convergence}
#| fig-cap: "Convergence of the cutoff interval"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
relw |>
  mutate(w = factor(sprintf("%.3f", w)), n = factor(n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(B, rel, colour = w, linetype = w, shape = w,
             group = interaction(w, n))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linewidth = 0.4, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(100, 400, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000),
                labels = c("100", "400", "1000", "2000", "5000", "10 000")) +
  scale_bw("Interval width", colours = pal_ramp5) +
  labs(x = "Bootstrap iterations (B), log scale",
       y = "Width relative to B = 10 000") +
  theme_paper(11)
```

*Note.* Median cutoff interval width at each number of iterations, relative to the width at 10 000 iterations of the same bootstrap, for four sample sizes and five interval widths. Each line is one combination of width and sample size, with the width shown by line type and point shape. Lines of the same width overlap, showing that convergence does not depend on sample size. Values below 1 indicate an interval narrower than its nominal width.

Second, the number of iterations required grows sharply as the interval widens. Taking 99% of that reference width as a criterion, `r bq(0.95)` iterations suffice for $w$ = .95, `r bq(0.99)` for $w$ = .99, and `r bq(0.999)` for $w$ = .999. The reference is empirical rather than asymptotic: at $w$ = .999 it has only five draws per tail itself, so the shortfall reported for that width is if anything understated. At 100 iterations the .999 interval reaches only `r rw(0.999, 100)` of that reference, that is roughly a quarter too narrow, while the .95 interval is already within `r short(0.95, 100)`%. This is the pattern that the expected number of draws per tail, $(1 - w)B/2$, predicts. Widths near 1 place their endpoints far into the tails of the simulated distribution, where few or no simulated values fall, so the interval collapses toward the range of the simulation.

## Error rates of the interval rule

@fig-fwe shows the familywise false positive rate under the null conditions, for all three item sets, against the prediction of @eq-fwer. At iteration counts where the interval has converged, the prediction describes the observed rates well. For the widths .90 to .99 at 2000 iterations, the ratio of observed to predicted rates ranges from `r sprintf("%.2f", min(conv_ok$ratio))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(conv_ok$ratio))` across all three item sets, with most values slightly below 1. The mild conservatism is expected, since item fit statistics are positively dependent through the shared total score and @eq-fwer assumes independence. The interval width therefore sets the familywise error rate of the decision rule, and it does so consistently across 9, 15, and 20 items and across dichotomous and polytomous formats.

The relation also holds below that range, where it is most exposed. On a five-item polytomous scale @eq-fwer predicts markedly lower rates of 41.0, 22.6, 4.9, 2.5 and 0.5% for the five widths, so a bound that was loose because of dependence among item statistics would show it here. From `r fmt_n(reps5)` null replications per condition at $B$ = 2000, the observed rates were `r s5(600)` at $n$ = 600 and `r s5(250)` at $n$ = 250. No width departs from its prediction by more than `r sprintf("%.1f", maxz5)` Monte Carlo standard errors at either sample size, and at $n$ = 600 the two widest intervals fall below their predictions, the same mild conservatism seen at 9, 15, and 20 items. Equation 1 therefore describes five-item scales as well as longer ones.

```{r fig-fwe}
#| fig-cap: "Familywise false positive rate against the prediction of @eq-fwer"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
fwe |>
  mutate(arm = factor(arm, levels = c("9 phq9", "15 polytomous",
                                      "20 dichotomous"),
                      labels = c("9 phq9 items", "15 polytomous items",
                                      "20 dichotomous items"))) |>
  mutate(w = factor(sprintf("%.3f", w))) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(B), obs, colour = w, linetype = w, shape = w, group = w)) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = pred), colour = "grey65",
             linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  facet_wrap(~arm, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(angle = 45)) +
  scale_bw("Interval width", colours = pal_ramp5) +
  labs(x = "Bootstrap iterations (B)",
       y = "Familywise false positives (%)") +
  theme_paper(12) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,100))
```

*Note.* Rates under the null conditions, by interval width and number of iterations, for the three item sets. Dotted grey horizontal lines are the predictions of @eq-fwer, one for each width. Observed rates approach the prediction as the interval converges, and exceed it when too few iterations leave the interval narrower than its nominal width.

Where the interval has not converged, the observed rates lie above the prediction, and by a wide margin at the narrowest widths. For the 20 dichotomous items at $w$ = .999, whose nominal familywise error rate is `r pq("20 dichotomous", 0.999)`%, the observed rate was `r fq("20 dichotomous", 0.999, 100)`% at 100 iterations and `r fq("20 dichotomous", 0.999, 400)`% at 400. Even at 2000 iterations it remained `r fq("20 dichotomous", 0.999, 2000)`%, which is consistent with the interval still being `r short(0.999, 2000, 1)`% narrower than the reference at that point. The two studies thus tell one story from two directions. A small shortfall in interval width translates into a large excess in familywise error, because the error rate is governed by the extreme tails that the shortfall affects.

## The detection and false positive trade-off across iterations

The recommendation of 100 to 400 iterations in Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025] rested on the observation that detection rates were highest with the fewest iterations. The present results show the same trade-off and explain its source. With three misfitting items among 20 dichotomous items at $n$ = 150, detection across 100, 200, 400, 1000, and 2000 iterations was `r aq(150, "det")`%, a decline of the same magnitude as the one reported in the earlier paper. The false positive rate on the fitting items in the same conditions was `r aq(150, "fp", 1)`%, and the familywise false positive rate under the null fell from `r fq("20 dichotomous", 0.999, 100)`% to `r fq("20 dichotomous", 0.999, 2000)`% over the same range. The decline in detection appears only where detection is not already at ceiling. With a single misfitting item in the same item set, detection stayed at or above `r sprintf("%.1f", min(k1det$det))`% at every number of iterations, and only the false positive rate responded.

Detection and false positives therefore decline together, and for the same reason. Fewer iterations produce a narrower interval, a narrower interval flags more items, and among the flagged items are both misfitting and fitting ones. The apparent advantage of few iterations was not greater sensitivity but a lower and undocumented threshold. Since the earlier paper evaluated false positives per item rather than across the scale, the cost was easy to overlook. A per-item rate of `r sprintf("%.0f", ART$fp[ART$n == 150 & ART$B == 100])`% at 100 iterations is unremarkable in isolation, while the corresponding probability of at least one false flag somewhere in a 20-item scale was `r fq("20 dichotomous", 0.999, 100)`%.

# Interval-based versus p-value-based decisions

```{r r5-prep}
#| include: false
al5 <- 0.05
GP <- bind_part(s_grid, "pval", c("rep", "k", "n"))

# null familywise error by rule and B, pooled over n (dichotomous, 20 items).
# Holm from the marginal p-values within each analysis. wyj = Westfall-Young
# with the observed and simulated statistics studentized jointly over all
# B + 1 values (computed in rev1/fresh_rerun.R from the same draws).
G0p <- GP |>
  filter(k == 0) |>
  mutate(p_holm = p.adjust(p_marg, "holm"), .by = c(rep, n, B))
null_any <- G0p |>
  mutate(unc = p_marg < al5, holm = p_holm < al5, wy = padj_fwer < al5,
         wyj = padj_fwer_pool < al5, bh = padj_bh < al5) |>
  summarise(across(c(unc, holm, wy, wyj, bh), any), .by = c(rep, n, B))
null_rules <- null_any |>
  summarise(across(c(unc, holm, wy, wyj, bh), ~100 * mean(.x)), .by = B) |>
  arrange(B)

# paired standard-minus-joint Westfall-Young difference per B
wyj_pair <- null_any |>
  mutate(d = as.numeric(wy) - as.numeric(wyj)) |>
  summarise(diff = 100 * mean(d), se = 100 * sd(d) / sqrt(n()), .by = B) |>
  arrange(B)
wjd <- function(B_, col = "diff") sprintf("%.1f", wyj_pair[[col]][wyj_pair$B == B_])
wjd_max_from <- function(from) sprintf("%.1f",
  max(abs(wyj_pair$diff[wyj_pair$B >= from])))

# per-item rejection rate of the marginal test under the null, against the
# largest size a valid Monte Carlo test can attain at that B
item_rate <- G0p |>
  summarise(rate = 100 * mean(p_marg < al5), .by = B) |>
  mutate(attain = 100 * floor(al5 * (B + 1) - 1e-9) / (B + 1))
ir_rng <- sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", min(item_rate$rate), max(item_rate$rate))

# Westfall-Young null rate in the polytomous studies, pooled, from B = 400
poly_wy0 <- bind_part(s_poly, "pval", c("arm", "rep", "k", "n", "rho")) |>
  filter(k == 0) |>
  summarise(any = any(padj_fwer < al5, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(arm, rep, n, B)) |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(any), .by = B)
pw_rng <- with(poly_wy0[poly_wy0$B >= 400, ],
               sprintf("%.1f and %.1f", min(pct), max(pct)))
nr <- function(col, B_) sprintf("%.1f", null_rules[[col]][null_rules$B == B_])
nr_rng <- function(col, from) {
  v <- null_rules[[col]][null_rules$B >= from]
  sprintf("%.1f and %.1f", min(v), max(v))
}
n_null <- GP |> filter(k == 0) |> distinct(rep, n, B) |> count(B) |> pull(n) |> unique()
stopifnot(length(n_null) == 1)

# BH, Holm and WY detection by B for k = 1 and k = 3 at n = 150. Holm is
# adjusted over all 20 items of each analysis before keeping the misfitting ones.
seqs <- GP |>
  filter(k > 0, n == 150) |>
  mutate(is_mis = mapply(function(k, it) it %in% s_grid$misfit[seq_len(k)],
                         k, item)) |>
  mutate(p_holm = p.adjust(p_marg, "holm"), .by = c(rep, k, n, B)) |>
  filter(is_mis) |>
  summarise(bh = 100 * mean(padj_bh < al5, na.rm = TRUE),
            holm = 100 * mean(p_holm < al5, na.rm = TRUE),
            wy = 100 * mean(padj_fwer < al5, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(k, B)) |>
  arrange(k, B)
sq <- function(k_, rule_) paste(sprintf("%.0f", seqs[[rule_]][seqs$k == k_]),
                                collapse = ", ")

# anchored misfit level: all rules, both arms, rho = .85
RH <- bind_part(s_poly, "hdci", c("arm", "rep", "k", "n", "rho")) |>
  filter(abs(rho - 0.85) < 1e-9, k > 0)
RP <- bind_part(s_poly, "pval", c("arm", "rep", "k", "n", "rho")) |>
  filter(abs(rho - 0.85) < 1e-9, k > 0)
mis5 <- function(a, k) s_poly$arms[[a]]$mis[seq_len(k)]

r5_all <- bind_rows(
  RH |> filter(abs(w - 0.999) < 1e-9) |>
    transmute(arm, rep, k, n, B, item, flag = as.integer(code > 0),
              rule = "Interval, w = .999"),
  RP |> transmute(arm, rep, k, n, B, item, flag = as.integer(p_marg < al5),

  RP |> transmute(arm, rep, k, n, B, item,
                  flag = as.integer(padj_fwer < al5), rule = "Westfall-Young"),
  RP |> transmute(arm, rep, k, n, B, item,
                  flag = as.integer(padj_bh < al5), rule = "Benjamini-Hochberg"),
  # Holm from the marginal p-values, adjusted over all items of each analysis
  RP |> mutate(p_holm = p.adjust(p_marg, "holm"), .by = c(arm, rep, k, n, B)) |>
    transmute(arm, rep, k, n, B, item, flag = as.integer(p_holm < al5),

) |>
  mutate(is_mis = mapply(function(a, k, it) it %in% mis5(a, k), arm, k, item),

                       levels = c("phq9, n = 150", "phq9, n = 250",

# and in the appendix table of decision rules.
r5 <- r5_all |> filter(rule != "Holm")

# pooled false positives at B = 2000 by rule

  filter(B == 2000, !is_mis) |>
  summarise(fp = 100 * mean(flag, na.rm = TRUE), .by = rule)
```
