```{r r5-prep}
fp2000_h <- r5_all |>
  filter(B == 2000, !is_mis, rule == "Holm") |>
  summarise(fp = 100 * mean(flag, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull(fp)

# Holm against Westfall-Young at the anchored level: detection at B = 100,
# and the paired detection difference at B = 2000
holm100 <- r5_all |>
  filter(B == 100, is_mis, rule == "Holm") |>
  summarise(det = 100 * mean(flag)) |> pull(det)
holm_gain <- r5_all |>
  filter(B == 2000, is_mis, rule %in% c("Holm", "Westfall-Young")) |>
  summarise(d = mean(flag), .by = c(arm, k, n, rep, rule)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rule, values_from = d) |>
  mutate(diff = 100 * (`Westfall-Young` - Holm)) |>
  summarise(gain = mean(diff), se = sd(diff) / sqrt(n()), .by = c(arm, k, n))
hg_rng <- sprintf("%.1f and %.1f", min(holm_gain$gain), max(holm_gain$gain))
hg_se <- sprintf("%.1f", max(holm_gain$se))

# detection gain of WY over the interval at w = .999 and the matched w = .995,
# phq9 arm, B = 2000, paired within replications
gain_vs <- function(wv) {
  M <- inner_join(
    RH |> filter(abs(w - wv) < 1e-9, arm == "phq9", B == 2000) |>
      mutate(h = as.integer(code > 0)) |> select(rep, k, n, item, h),
    RP |> filter(arm == "phq9", B == 2000) |>
      mutate(f = as.integer(padj_fwer < al5)) |> select(rep, k, n, item, f),
    by = c("rep", "k", "n", "item")) |>
    mutate(is_mis = mapply(function(k, it) it %in% mis5("phq9", k), k, item))
  M |> filter(is_mis) |>
    summarise(g = 100 * (mean(f) - mean(h)), .by = c(k, n))
}
g999 <- gain_vs(0.999); g995 <- gain_vs(0.995)
rng <- function(g) sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", min(g$g[g$g > 1]), max(g$g))

# matched-width null check: observed familywise error of w = .995 for 9 items
H0 <- bind_part(s_poly, "hdci", c("arm", "rep", "k", "n", "rho")) |>
  filter(k == 0, arm == "phq9", B == 2000, abs(w - 0.995) < 1e-9)
fwe995 <- 100 * mean(
  (H0 |> summarise(a = any(code > 0), .by = c(rep, n)))$a)
```

## The four rules compared

The p-value rules are first examined under the null conditions of the dichotomous study, where any flag is a false positive. @tbl-null-rules shows the familywise error rate by rule and number of iterations, pooled over the four sample sizes. Three patterns stand out. Scanning all 20 items with uncorrected marginal p-values produces a familywise error rate around 60% at every $B$, which is the expected consequence of testing 20 hypotheses at $\alpha$ = .05 and the reason a correction is needed. The WY step-down is mildly liberal at $B$ = 100, at `r nr('wy', 100)`%, falls to `r nr('wy', 200)`% at $B$ = 200, and from $B$ = 400 it is stable and slightly below its nominal 5%, between `r nr_rng('wy', 400)`% up to $B$ = 10 000. The near-zero Holm and BH rates at $B$ = 100 and 200 are explained by the reachability floor of @eq-bhfloor: with 20 comparisons a single standout cannot be flagged below $B$ = 400. BH can flag below that when several items sit at the Monte Carlo floor at once, which is rare under the null, and Holm flagged nothing. From $B$ = 400 Holm was between `r nr_rng('holm', 400)`% and BH between `r nr_rng('bh', 400)`%.

```{r tbl-null-rules}
#| tbl-cap: "Familywise error rate of the p-value decision rules"
knitr::kable(null_rules, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("B", "Uncorrected", "Holm", "WY",
                           "WY, joint", "BH"))
```

*Note.* Percentages under the null conditions of the dichotomous study (20 items, no misfitting items), by number of bootstrap iterations. Pooled over the four sample sizes, `r fmt_n(n_null)` datasets per cell. Uncorrected is the marginal p-value of @eq-pmarg. WY is the Westfall-Young step-down, WY, joint the same step-down with the observed and simulated statistics studentized together over all $B + 1$ values, computed from the same bootstrap, and BH the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. All values of $B$ within a replication come from one bootstrap of 10 000 iterations.

The decline of the WY rate between $B$ = 100 and 400 is the studentization effect described in the section on bootstrap p-values. With joint studentization the rate was between `r nr_rng('wyj', 100)`% at every $B$, and paired within replications the standard version exceeded the joint one by `r wjd(100)` percentage points at $B$ = 100 (SE `r wjd(100, 'se')`) and by at most `r wjd_max_from(1000)` points from $B$ = 1000. The excess at small $B$ is therefore a property of the studentization rather than of the step-down.

What remains is a level slightly below 5% that does not change between $B$ = 400 and 10 000 under either version, and the per-item marginal tests flagged `r ir_rng`% of fitting items at every $B$. An error that does not shrink as $B$ grows is not Monte Carlo error but the finite-sample departure that Ferreira [-@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024, Section 5] notes for bootstrap methods with estimated parameters, here conservative. It was smaller in the polytomous studies, at `r pw_rng`% from $B$ = 400.

The reachability floor also shapes detection. With a single misfitting item at $n$ = 150, BH detection across $B$ = 100 to 2000 was `r sq(1, "bh")`%, jumping exactly where $B$ crosses the floor of 400. With three misfitting items the sequence was `r sq(3, "bh")`%, with substantial detection already at $B$ = 200, because three p-values at the Monte Carlo floor lower the attainable adjusted p-value to $m/(3(B+1))$. Holm detected nothing below its floor in either condition (`r sq(1, "holm")`% and `r sq(3, "holm")`%), since several standouts do not lower it. The WY rule was flat across the whole range at `r sq(1, "wy")`% and `r sq(3, "wy")`% respectively, since it needs only $B \geq 20$ to reject and its power does not depend on $B$ beyond that.

```{r fig-rules}
#| fig-cap: "Detection and false positives for the four decision rules"
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 4.8
r5 |>
  mutate(metric = ifelse(is_mis, "Detection (%)", "False positives (%)")) |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(flag, na.rm = TRUE),
            .by = c(rule, cond, B, metric)) |>
  mutate(rule = factor(rule, levels = c("Westfall-Young", "Benjamini-Hochberg",
                                        "Interval, w = .999", "Marginal p"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(B), pct, colour = rule, linetype = rule, shape = rule,
             group = rule)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  facet_grid(metric ~ cond, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_bw("Decision rule", colours = pal_rules) +
  labs(x = "Bootstrap iterations (B)", y = NULL) +
  theme_paper(13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.6, "cm")) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2), shape = guide_legend(nrow = 2),
         linetype = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

*Note.* Detection rate (misfitting items) and false positive rate (fitting items) at the anchored misfit level, by number of iterations, item set, and sample size. Rates are averaged over the misfitting-item conditions. Note the different y-axis scales for the two rows.

@fig-rules compares all four rules at the anchored misfit level. Against the interval at $w$ = .999 the WY rule detects substantially more misfit, by `r rng(g999)` percentage points across the non-saturated nine-item conditions at $B$ = 2000, at a false positive rate of `r fpv("Westfall-Young")`% against `r fpv("Interval, w = .999")`% for the interval, pooled across arms, so it detects more at a higher cost. Part of this raw gain, however, reflects the interval's implicit error rate rather than the method. By @eq-fwer, $w$ = .999 corresponds to a familywise rate of only 0.9% for nine items, so the interval is operating far below the $\alpha$ = .05 of the p-value rules.

A fair comparison holds the error rate constant. For nine items, $w$ = .995 implies a familywise rate of 4.4% by @eq-fwer, and its observed null rate at $B$ = 2000 was `r sprintf("%.1f", fwe995)`%, closely matching the p-value rules. Against this matched interval the WY rule still detected more misfit in every non-saturated condition, by `r rng(g995)` percentage points, with slightly fewer false positives. The remaining advantage comes from studentization and from using the joint distribution of the item statistics. More important than its size is what the matching exercise reveals: an interval width that matches a chosen $\alpha$ must be solved from @eq-fwer for each item count, and for most item counts no convenient width exists. The WY rule targets $\alpha$ directly, whatever the number of items.

@tbl-rules-appendix reports Holm by condition. At $B$ = 100 it detected `r sprintf("%.1f", holm100)`% of the misfitting items, since the floor of @eq-bhfloor is `r 9 / 0.05` iterations for nine items and `r 15 / 0.05` for fifteen. At $B$ = 2000 the WY rule detected between `r hg_rng` percentage points more than Holm across conditions, paired within replications, with standard errors of up to `r hg_se` points, and the pooled false positive rates were `r fpv("Westfall-Young")`% against `r sprintf("%.1f", fp2000_h)`%. Using the joint distribution of the item statistics therefore adds little power here, as Ferreira's [-@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024] account leads one to expect for statistics that are close to independent. The practical advantage of the step-down over Holm is that it needs no minimum number of iterations.

A short scale tests BH where the floor does not bind at all. At five items the floor is `r floor(5 / 0.05)` iterations, so the procedure operates freely at every $B$ examined, and the comparison is no longer handicapped by reachability. At $n$ = 250 it detected the misfitting item in `r bh5(250, "det_bh")`% of replications against `r bh5(250, "det_wy")`% for the WY rule, with false positives of `r bh5(250, "fp_bh")`% against `r bh5(250, "fp_wy")`%. At $n$ = 600 both detected it in every replication, with false positives of `r bh5(600, "fp_bh")`% against `r bh5(600, "fp_wy")`%. Paired within replications, the detection difference was within one standard error of zero at both sample sizes while the false positive difference exceeded four. The preference for the WY rule is therefore not an artifact of testing BH only where its floor binds.

BH and WY performed similarly with a single misfitting item, while with several misfitting items BH detected somewhat more, as expected since the false discovery rate is a more permissive criterion when true effects are present. The price appears on the other side of the ledger, with pooled false positives of `r fpv("Benjamini-Hochberg")`% against `r fpv("Westfall-Young")`% at $B$ = 2000, roughly a doubling. The marginal p-value, finally, is close to its nominal level per item but unusable as a screening rule, as its familywise rate of around 60% shows. Once items misfit its false positive rate on the fitting items rises, which the section on error rates under misfit returns to. Taken together, these results support the WY p-value as the default among the decision rules examined, with Holm a close alternative once $B$ clears its floor, the marginal p-value reserved for a single pre-specified item, and BH for longer instruments where a false discovery criterion is acceptable and $B$ clears the reachability floor. The interval retains descriptive value, which the Discussion returns to.

## Conditional outfit under the same rules

```{r outfit-prep}
#| include: false
R6 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(s_stat$grid)), function(i) {
  r <- s_stat$res[[i]]
  if (is.null(r)) return(NULL)
  g <- s_stat$grid[i, c("arm", "target", "n", "rep"), drop = FALSE]
  rownames(g) <- NULL
  cbind(g, r)
})) |>
  mutate(is_mis = mis > 0 & item == mis,
         f_in  = as.integer(padj_infit  < 0.05),
         f_out = as.integer(padj_outfit < 0.05),
         f_any = as.integer(f_in == 1 | f_out == 1))

r6 <- function(v) sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", min(v), max(v))
english_n <- function(x) c("one", "two", "three", "four",
  "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine", "ten")[x]

# familywise error and marginal calibration under the null
null6 <- R6 |>
  filter(target == "none") |>
  summarise(infit  = as.integer(sum(f_in)  > 0),
            outfit = as.integer(sum(f_out) > 0),
            union  = as.integer(sum(f_any) > 0), .by = c(arm, n, rep)) |>
  summarise(across(c(infit, outfit, union), \(x) 100 * mean(x)), .by = c(arm, n))
marg6 <- R6 |>
  filter(target == "none") |>
  summarise(infit = 100 * mean(p_infit < 0.05),
            outfit = 100 * mean(p_outfit < 0.05), .by = c(arm, n))
mcse6 <- 100 * sqrt(0.05 * 0.95 / 250)

# achieved misfit on both scales
inj6 <- R6 |>
  filter(is_mis) |>
  summarise(infit = mean(infit_msq), outfit = mean(outfit_msq), .by = arm)
inj <- function(a, s) sprintf("%.2f", inj6[[s]][inj6$arm == a])

# detection and paired discordance on the misfitting item
det6 <- R6 |>
  filter(is_mis) |>
  summarise(det_in = 100 * mean(f_in), det_out = 100 * mean(f_out),
            only_in = sum(f_in == 1 & f_out == 0),
            only_out = sum(f_in == 0 & f_out == 1),
            reps = n(), .by = c(arm, target, n))
n_win <- sum(det6$det_out > det6$det_in)          # conditions where outfit wins
gap6 <- det6$det_in - det6$det_out
gap_on  <- gap6[det6$target == "on"]
gap_off <- gap6[det6$target == "off"]

# null variability of the two statistics, and how it grows off target
sd6 <- R6 |>
  filter(target == "none") |>
  summarise(ratio = sd(outfit_msq) / sd(infit_msq), .by = c(arm, n))
sdr <- function(a) sprintf("%.1f", mean(sd6$ratio[sd6$arm == a]))
sd_loc <- R6 |>
  filter(target == "none", arm == "dich20", n == 600) |>
  mutate(loc = abs(s_stat$arms$dich20$locs[item])) |>
  summarise(ratio = sd(outfit_msq) / sd(infit_msq), loc = first(loc), .by = item)
sd_cen <- sprintf("%.1f", mean(sd_loc$ratio[rank(sd_loc$loc) <= 5]))
sd_ext <- sprintf("%.1f", mean(sd_loc$ratio[rank(-sd_loc$loc) <= 5]))
```

Every result so far concerns conditional infit. The same bootstrap produces conditional outfit at no additional cost, and the decision rules are indifferent to which statistic they are given, so it is worth asking whether anything is gained by reading both. Outfit is also widely reported in its unconditional form, for example by RUMM2030, a widely used Rasch analysis software package. The comparison here concerns conditional outfit only, and its results need not carry over to the unconditional statistic, whose behavior under the model differs [@muller_item_2020]. Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025] compared conditional infit and outfit for dichotomous items under the interval rule and found outfit worse throughout. The sixth study revisits that comparison under the corrected p-value and extends it to polytomous items. The two item sets were placed at correlations that inject comparable infit, `r inj("dich20", "infit")` for the dichotomous set and `r inj("phq9", "infit")` for the phq9 set, both inside the range the real phq9 items reach. A single misfitting item was placed either near the person mean or off target, the WY rule was applied at $B$ = 1000 and $\alpha$ = .05, and both statistics were read from the same bootstrap within each replication.

Under the null conditions the FWER was `r r6(null6$outfit)`% for outfit against `r r6(null6$infit)`% for infit, across the four combinations of item set and sample size, with a Monte Carlo standard error of `r sprintf("%.1f", mcse6)` points. The marginal rates before the step-down were `r r6(marg6$outfit)`% and `r r6(marg6$infit)`%. Neither the statistic nor the correction is miscalibrated, so the studentized maximum needs no modification when the statistic it is given changes.

Detection is a different matter. Infit detected the misfitting item more often than outfit in every one of the `r english_n(nrow(det6))` conditions, and @tbl-outfit gives the margins. The gap is not small, ranging from `r sprintf("%.0f", min(gap6))` to `r sprintf("%.0f", max(gap6))` percentage points. Outfit is the unweighted mean of squared standardized residuals and is conventionally expected to earn its place on items far from the person mean, and the injected outfit is indeed larger there. Detection nevertheless moves the other way. Averaged over item sets and sample sizes the infit advantage was `r sprintf("%.0f", mean(gap_on))` points for the on-target item and `r sprintf("%.0f", mean(gap_off))` points for the off-target one. The null conditions explain why. Outfit is the more variable statistic under a true model, by a factor of `r sdr("dich20")` in the dichotomous set and `r sdr("phq9")` in the phq9 set, and within the dichotomous set that factor is `r sd_cen` for the five most central items and `r sd_ext` for the five most extreme. The variance grows faster than the signal exactly where outfit was expected to help.

Because both statistics come from the same bootstrap, the comparison can be made replication by replication rather than only on the margins. @tbl-outfit reports the discordant counts. Replications in which outfit flagged the misfitting item and infit did not never exceeded `r max(det6$only_out)` of 250, against up to `r max(det6$only_in)` in the other direction, and every condition favours infit at $p$ < .01 by an exact test on the discordant pairs. In these conditions outfit added little to what infit detected.

This has a direct consequence for practice, because both statistics often appear side by side in the standard output. Flagging an item when either statistic is significant tests 2$k$ hypotheses while each correction covers $k$, and the null FWER of that combined rule was `r r6(null6$union)`%, against a nominal 5% and the `r r6(c(null6$infit, null6$outfit))`% the two statistics reach on their own. The inflation is below the doubling that independent statistics would produce, since the two are computed on the same responses and are positively dependent, but it is real and adds almost no detection. For conditional statistics at these settings, the results favor deciding on infit and treating outfit as descriptive.

```{r tbl-outfit}
#| tbl-cap: "Detection and paired disagreement, conditional infit versus outfit"
det6 |>
  mutate(Items = ifelse(arm == "dich20", "20 dich", "9 phq9"),
         Target = ifelse(target == "on", "On target", "Off target"),
         p = mapply(function(a, b) if (a + b == 0L) NA_real_ else
                      stats::binom.test(a, a + b, 0.5)$p.value,
                    only_out, only_in),
         p = ifelse(is.na(p), "-", ifelse(p < 0.001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", p)))) |>
  arrange(Items, desc(Target), n) |>
  select(Items, Target, n, det_in, det_out, only_in, only_out, p) |>
  collapse_keys(c("Items", "Target")) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, align = "llrrrrrr",
               col.names = c("Items", "Target", "n", "Det infit", "Det outfit",
                             "Only infit", "Only outfit", "p"))
```

*Note.* Westfall-Young (WY) rule at $B$ = 1000 and $\alpha$ = .05, 250 replications per condition. Det is the percentage of replications in which the misfitting item was flagged. Only infit and Only outfit count the replications in which one statistic flagged it and the other did not. The p-value is an exact binomial test on those discordant counts. Design and false positive rates are in @tbl-outfit-appendix.

## Random responding under the same rules

```{r mech-prep}
#| include: false
mism <- s_mech$mis
LH <- bind_part(s_mech, "hdci", c("rep", "k", "n")) |>
  filter(abs(w - 0.999) < 1e-9) |>
  mutate(mech = "noise") |> select(mech, rep, k, n, B, item, code)
LP <- bind_part(s_mech, "pval", c("rep", "k", "n")) |>
  mutate(mech = "noise") |> select(mech, rep, k, n, B, item, padj_fwer)
XH <- bind_part(s_poly, "hdci", c("arm", "rep", "k", "n", "rho")) |>
  filter(arm == "phq9", abs(rho - 0.85) < 1e-9, abs(w - 0.999) < 1e-9) |>
  mutate(mech = "dim") |> select(mech, rep, k, n, B, item, code)
XP <- bind_part(s_poly, "pval", c("arm", "rep", "k", "n", "rho")) |>
  filter(arm == "phq9", abs(rho - 0.85) < 1e-9) |>
  mutate(mech = "dim") |> select(mech, rep, k, n, B, item, padj_fwer)

# false positives on the fitting items, two misfitting items, n = 1000, B = 2000
fp_h <- bind_rows(LH, XH) |>
  filter(k == 2, n == 1000, B == 2000, !(item %in% mism)) |>
  summarise(fp = 100 * mean(code > 0), .by = mech)
fp_p <- bind_rows(LP, XP) |>
  filter(k == 2, n == 1000, B == 2000, !(item %in% mism)) |>
  summarise(fp = 100 * mean(padj_fwer < al5, na.rm = TRUE), .by = mech)
mq <- function(d, m) sprintf("%.1f", d$fp[d$mech == m])

# direction of the false flags under the interval rule, pooled over conditions
dir_m <- bind_rows(LH, XH) |>
  filter(k > 0, !(item %in% mism), code > 0) |>
  summarise(over = 100 * mean(code == 1), .by = mech)
oq <- function(m) sprintf("%.0f", dir_m$over[dir_m$mech == m])

# detection of the two target items at n = 250
det_m <- bind_rows(LP, XP) |>
  filter(k == 2, n == 250, B == 2000, item %in% mism) |>
  summarise(det = 100 * mean(padj_fwer < al5, na.rm = TRUE), .by = mech)
dq <- function(m) sprintf("%.1f", det_m$det[det_m$mech == m])
```

Every result so far induces misfit through multidimensionality, so two of them could in principle be properties of that mechanism rather than of misfit in general. The first is the false positives that appear on fitting items once misfitting items are present. The second is the masking that weakens detection when two items misfit together. The mechanism check separates the two. It holds the item set, the conditions and the decision rules fixed, and replaces multidimensionality with random responding at matched infit.

The false positives are not specific to multidimensionality. With two misfitting items at $n$ = 1000 and $B$ = 2000, random responding produced false positives on the seven fitting items of `r mq(fp_h, "noise")`% under the interval rule at $w$ = .999 and `r mq(fp_p, "noise")`% under the WY rule, against `r mq(fp_h, "dim")`% and `r mq(fp_p, "dim")`% under multidimensionality. Nearly all false flags pointed in the overfit direction under the interval rule for both mechanisms, at `r oq("noise")`% and `r oq("dim")`% of flags. Direction is read from the band, so the p-value rules cannot be scored the same way. What puts a fitting item outside its expected range is contamination of the total score that it is conditioned on, rather than the particular way that contamination arises. The error rate results are therefore not an artifact of the mechanism, and the multidimensional condition is the more forgiving of the two.

Masking is mechanism-specific, and should be read as such. Two independently noisy items do not mask each other, and detection of the two target items at $n$ = 250 was `r dq("noise")`% under random responding against `r dq("dim")`% under multidimensionality. Masking requires the misfitting items to share a source. That is the case worth planning for, since a secondary dimension rarely involves a single item, but it is not a property of misfit in general.

## Error rates when some items misfit

```{r partial-prep}
#| include: false
# Familywise error over the fitting items (any fitting item flagged) and the
# false discovery proportion, per replication, at B = 2000, for every
# condition with misfitting items. Holm is computed from the marginal p-values
# where the study stored them (not in the mechanism check).
per_rep_err <- function(L, keys) {
  L |>
    summarise(fp = sum(flag[!is_mis]), tp = sum(flag[is_mis]),
              .by = all_of(c(keys, "rep", "rule"))) |>
    mutate(any_fp = fp > 0, fdp = ifelse(fp + tp > 0, fp / (fp + tp), 0)) |>
    summarise(fwer = 100 * mean(any_fp), fdr = 100 * mean(fdp),
              .by = all_of(c(keys, "rule")))
}
# polytomous studies at the anchored level
PE <- r5_all |>
  filter(B == 2000, !is.na(flag)) |>
  per_rep_err(c("arm", "k", "n")) |>
  mutate(set = ifelse(arm == "phq9", "9 phq9", "15 polytomous"))
# dichotomous study (rho = .15), fresh data
GPm <- GP |>
  filter(k > 0, B == 2000) |>
  mutate(p_holm = p.adjust(p_marg, "holm"), .by = c(rep, k, n, B),
         is_mis = mapply(function(k, it) it %in% s_grid$misfit[seq_len(k)], k, item))
DE <- bind_rows(
  GPm |> transmute(k, n, rep, item, is_mis, rule = "Holm", flag = p_holm < al5),
  GPm |> transmute(k, n, rep, item, is_mis, rule = "Westfall-Young", flag = padj_fwer < al5),
  GPm |> transmute(k, n, rep, item, is_mis, rule = "Benjamini-Hochberg", flag = padj_bh < al5)
) |>
  per_rep_err(c("k", "n")) |>
  mutate(set = "20 dichotomous")
# mechanism check, random responding in the phq9 set
ME <- bind_part(s_mech, "pval", c("rep", "k", "n")) |>
  filter(B == 2000) |>
  mutate(is_mis = mapply(function(k, it) it %in% mism[seq_len(k)], k, item))
ME <- bind_rows(
  ME |> transmute(k, n, rep, item, is_mis, rule = "Westfall-Young", flag = padj_fwer < al5),
  ME |> transmute(k, n, rep, item, is_mis, rule = "Benjamini-Hochberg", flag = padj_bh < al5)
) |>
  filter(!is.na(flag)) |>
  per_rep_err(c("k", "n")) |>
  mutate(set = "9 phq9, random responding")
partial <- bind_rows(PE |> select(-arm), DE, ME) |>
  filter(rule %in% c("Holm", "Westfall-Young", "Benjamini-Hochberg"))
pe <- function(set_, k_, n_, rule_, col = "fwer") sprintf("%.1f",
  partial[[col]][partial$set == set_ & partial$k == k_ & partial$n == n_ &
                   partial$rule == rule_])
pe_rng <- function(set_, rule_, col, nmax) {
  v <- partial[[col]][partial$set %in% set_ & partial$rule == rule_ & partial$n <= nmax]
  sprintf("%.1f and %.1f", min(v), max(v))
}
# per-item false positive rate of the uncorrected marginal p-value on fitting
# items, phq9 at the anchored level, n = 1000, B = 2000
marg_fp <- r5_all |>
  filter(arm == "phq9", n == 1000, B == 2000, rule == "Marginal p", !is_mis) |>
  summarise(fp = 100 * mean(flag), .by = k)
mfp <- function(k_) sprintf("%.1f", marg_fp$fp[marg_fp$k == k_])
# Westfall-Young over fitting items at the strongest polytomous misfit level
wy75 <- bind_part(s_poly, "pval", c("arm", "rep", "k", "n", "rho")) |>
  filter(abs(rho - 0.75) < 1e-9, k > 0, B == 2000) |>
  mutate(is_mis = mapply(function(a, k, it) it %in% mis5(a, k), arm, k, item)) |>
  summarise(any = any(padj_fwer[!is_mis] < al5), .by = c(arm, k, n, rep)) |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(any), .by = c(arm, k, n))
```

The error rates reported so far were measured under the null. With misfitting items present, strong FWER control concerns the probability of flagging at least one fitting item, and BH targets the false discovery rate, the expected proportion of flagged items that in fact fit. @tbl-partial reports both for every condition with misfitting items, at $B$ = 2000.

At sample sizes of 250 or below the rates were close to nominal. At the anchored misfit level in the polytomous sets, the WY rate over the fitting items was between `r pe_rng(c("9 phq9", "15 polytomous"), "Westfall-Young", "fwer", 250)`%, and the false discovery rate of BH between `r pe_rng(c("9 phq9", "15 polytomous"), "Benjamini-Hochberg", "fdr", 250)`%. At $n$ = 1000 every procedure exceeded its nominal level. For the nine phq9 items, the WY rate over fitting items was `r pe("9 phq9", 1, 1000, "Westfall-Young")`% with one misfitting item and `r pe("9 phq9", 2, 1000, "Westfall-Young")`% with two, the Holm rate `r pe("9 phq9", 1, 1000, "Holm")`% and `r pe("9 phq9", 2, 1000, "Holm")`%, and the false discovery rate of BH `r pe("9 phq9", 1, 1000, "Benjamini-Hochberg", "fdr")`% and `r pe("9 phq9", 2, 1000, "Benjamini-Hochberg", "fdr")`%. The rates grew with misfit severity, reaching `r sprintf("%.1f", max(wy75$pct))`% for WY at $\rho$ = .75, and were higher under random responding, at `r pe("9 phq9, random responding", 2, 1000, "Westfall-Young")`% with two misfitting items at $n$ = 1000.

The source of the excess lies in the per-item tests rather than in the corrections. At $n$ = 1000 the uncorrected marginal p-value flagged `r mfp(1)`% of the fitting phq9 items with one misfitting item and `r mfp(2)`% with two, where a valid per-item test would flag about 5%. Each fitting item's statistic is conditioned on a total score that includes the misfitting items, so its distribution changes when they misfit, while the bootstrap reference is generated from a model in which all items fit. This is the failure of subset pivotality described earlier, and Ferreira [-@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024, p. 2] notes that a p-value can have the wrong distribution because the model is incorrect rather than because its null hypothesis is false. It also explains why Holm, which needs no pivotality condition but relies on valid marginal p-values, failed in the same conditions. The procedures studied here therefore provide weak FWER control, and no correction applied to these per-item tests can provide strong control once misfit contaminates the conditioning score. The contamination grows with sample size and misfit severity, and removing the most misfitting item before judging the rest reduces it.

The false discovery rate of BH stayed close to nominal where the per-item tests were close to valid and exceeded it where they were not, and the WY rule had a false discovery rate at or below it in every condition. The preference for a familywise criterion rests on the use of the analysis. A scale of 5 to 20 items is judged item by item, each flag leads to an item being considered for removal, and a single false flag changes the instrument. The false discovery rate is most useful when many hypotheses are tested and many discoveries are expected [@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024], which is rarely the case in item fit analysis.

# Decision stability

The previous sections report error rates averaged over many simulated datasets, but an analyst has one dataset, and two analysts who run the same analysis on it with different random seeds can reach different conclusions. To quantify how often, ten datasets per condition were held fixed and each was analyzed with 25 bootstrap seeds. The observed infit values are then fixed, and all variation between seeds is simulation noise.

For each item and dataset, the flag rate $p$ is the proportion of the 25 seeds in which the item was flagged, and an item is counted as unstable when $0 < p < 1$. Twenty-five seeds resolve $p$ in steps of 0.04, so the unstable counts below are lower bounds. Two analyses disagree when their sets of flagged items differ, and the probability of this is measured directly as the proportion of the 300 pairs of seeds that disagree,

$$
D = 1 - \frac{\sum_j \binom{c_j}{2}}{\binom{S}{2}},
$$ {#eq-disagree}

where $c_j$ is the number of seeds that produced the $j$-th distinct set of flagged items and $S$ = 25 is the number of seeds. $D$ is computed within each dataset, averaged over the ten datasets of a condition, and needs no assumption about how the items depend on each other. For a single item the corresponding probability is $2p(1 - p)$, the chance that one of two seeds flags the item and the other does not.

```{r stab-prep}
#| include: false
al <- 0.05
SP <- bind_part(s_stab, "pval", c("arm", "k", "rho", "n", "dataset", "seed")) |>
  mutate(rho = round(rho, 2))
SH <- bind_part(s_stab, "hdci", c("arm", "k", "rho", "n", "dataset", "seed")) |>
  filter(abs(w - 0.999) < 1e-9) |>
  mutate(rho = round(rho, 2))

rate_p <- SP |>
  summarise(p = mean(padj_fwer < al, na.rm = TRUE),
            .by = c(arm, k, rho, n, B, dataset, item)) |>
  mutate(rule = "FWER p-value")
rate_h <- SH |>
  summarise(p = mean(code > 0), .by = c(arm, k, rho, n, B, dataset, item)) |>
  mutate(rule = "Interval, w = .999")
rates <- bind_rows(rate_p, rate_h)

# pooled unstable percentages, anchored misfit (rho = .85, both arms and n)
pool85 <- rates |>
  filter(rho == 0.85, k > 0) |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(p > 0 & p < 1), .by = c(rule, B))
pf <- function(rule_, B_) sprintf("%.1f", pool85$pct[pool85$rule == rule_ & pool85$B == B_])

# pooled null (no misfitting items)
pool0 <- rates |>
  filter(k == 0, rule == "FWER p-value") |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(p > 0 & p < 1), .by = B)

# dataset-cluster bootstrap SE for the pooled anchored estimates (FWER)
set.seed(11)
p85f <- rates |> filter(rho == 0.85, k > 0, rule == "FWER p-value") |>
  mutate(cl = paste(arm, n, dataset))
boot_pool <- function(B_) {
  x <- p85f[p85f$B == B_, ]
  cls <- unique(x$cl)
  sd(replicate(300, {
    cs <- sample(cls, replace = TRUE)
    y <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cs, function(cc) x[x$cl == cc, ]))
    100 * mean(y$p > 0 & y$p < 1)
  }))
}
se400 <- boot_pool(400); se2000 <- boot_pool(2000)

# two-analyst disagreement measured from seed pairs (Equation 5): the share of
# the choose(S, 2) pairs of seeds whose sets of flagged items differ. Seeds
# with a missing item result are dropped. The independence product with the
# finite-seed correction S / (S - 1) is kept for comparison.
skeys <- c("rule", "arm", "k", "rho", "n", "B", "dataset")
SF <- bind_rows(
  SP |> transmute(arm, k, rho, n, dataset, seed, B, item,
                  rule = "FWER p-value", flag = as.integer(padj_fwer < al)),
  SH |> transmute(arm, k, rho, n, dataset, seed, B, item,
                  rule = "Interval, w = .999", flag = as.integer(code > 0))
) |>
  filter(!any(is.na(flag)), .by = all_of(c(skeys, "seed")))
D_emp <- SF |>
  arrange(item) |>
  summarise(pat = paste(flag, collapse = ""), .by = all_of(c(skeys, "seed"))) |>
  summarise(S = n(), D = 1 - sum(choose(table(pat), 2)) / choose(n(), 2),
            .by = all_of(skeys))
D_ind <- SF |>
  summarise(p = mean(flag), S = n(), .by = all_of(c(skeys, "item"))) |>
  summarise(D_ind = 1 - prod(1 - 2 * p * (1 - p) * S / (S - 1)),
            .by = all_of(skeys))
D_all <- left_join(D_emp, D_ind, by = skeys)
stopifnot(nrow(D_all) == nrow(D_emp), all(D_emp$S >= 20))

# pooled two-analyst disagreement (FWER), anchored misfit
dis <- D_all |>
  filter(rho == 0.85, k > 0, rule == "FWER p-value") |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(D), pct_ind = 100 * mean(D_ind), .by = B) |>
  arrange(B)
dv <- setNames(sprintf("%.0f", dis$pct), dis$B)
dis_gap <- sprintf("%.1f", max(abs(dis$pct - dis$pct_ind)))
# where independence fails: datasets in which the independence product
# overstates or understates the measured disagreement by more than 5 points
dep <- D_all |>
  filter(k > 0) |>
  summarise(N = n(), over = sum(D_ind - D > 0.05), under = sum(D_ind - D < -0.05),
            maxgap = 100 * max(abs(D_ind - D)), .by = rule)
dq_ <- function(rule_, col) dep[[col]][dep$rule == rule_]
# disagreement at B = 2000 across all misfit conditions (FWER)
dis_cond <- D_all |>
  filter(k > 0, rule == "FWER p-value", B == 2000) |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(D), .by = c(arm, rho, n))

# borderline-item counts per dataset at the strongest misfit, B = 2000
bord <- rate_p |>
  filter(B == 2000, rho == 0.15, k > 0) |>
  summarise(nb = sum(p > 0 & p < 1), .by = c(arm, n, dataset)) |>
  summarise(mb = mean(nb), .by = c(arm, n))
bb <- function(n_) sprintf("%.1f", mean(bord$mb[bord$n == n_]))

# unstable % per condition for the figure
unst <- rates |>
  filter(k > 0) |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(p > 0 & p < 1), .by = c(rule, arm, rho, n, B))
```

Under the null conditions, flagging with the WY p-value is essentially reproducible. Pooled across both item sets and sample sizes, `r sprintf("%.1f", pool0$pct[pool0$B == 100])`% of items had a seed-dependent flag at $B$ = 100, `r sprintf("%.1f", pool0$pct[pool0$B == 400])`% at $B$ = 400, and none at $B$ = 2000. At the anchored misfit level ($\rho$ = .85), pooled the same way, `r pf("FWER p-value", 400)`% of items were unstable at $B$ = 400 and `r pf("FWER p-value", 2000)`% at $B$ = 2000 (Monte Carlo standard error `r sprintf("%.1f", max(se400, se2000))` percentage points), against `r pf("Interval, w = .999", 400)`% and `r pf("Interval, w = .999", 2000)`% for the interval rule at $w$ = .999. Pooled at the anchored level, the probability that two seeds using the WY rule disagree about at least one item was `r dv["100"]`% at $B$ = 100, `r dv["400"]`% at $B$ = 400, `r dv["1000"]`% at $B$ = 1000, and `r dv["2000"]`% at $B$ = 2000. $B$ = 400 is thus where the error rates are trustworthy, but reproducibility keeps improving well past it.

Treating the items as flipping independently, with each $2p(1 - p)$ multiplied by $S/(S - 1)$ to remove the bias of estimating $p$ from 25 seeds, gives nearly the same pooled values, within `r dis_gap` percentage points. The average hides where independence fails. For the WY rule the independence product overstated the measured disagreement by more than 5 percentage points in `r dq_("FWER p-value", "over")` of `r dq_("FWER p-value", "N")` combinations of dataset and number of iterations, by up to `r sprintf("%.0f", dq_("FWER p-value", "maxgap"))` points, and `r if (dq_("FWER p-value", "under") == 0) "never understated it by as much" else paste("understated it by as much in", dq_("FWER p-value", "under"))`. In those datasets one seed's maximum statistic moves several decisions together, the coupling that the step-down introduces. For the interval rule, whose items are judged separately, the two agreed within `r sprintf("%.0f", dq_("Interval, w = .999", "maxgap"))` points in every dataset.

```{r fig-stability}
#| fig-cap: "Seed dependence of flagging decisions"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
unst |>
  mutate(rho = factor(sprintf("%.2f", rho))) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(B), pct, colour = rho, shape = rho, linetype = rule,
             group = interaction(rho, rule))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  facet_grid(arm ~ n, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_bw("Correlation", colours = rev(pal_ramp3), linetype = FALSE) +
  scale_linetype_manual(name = "Decision rule", values = c("solid", "42")) +
  labs(x = "Bootstrap iterations (B)", y = "Items with seed-dependent flag (%)") +
  theme_paper(12) +
  theme(legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.4, "cm"))
```

*Note.* Percentage of items whose flagging decision depends on the bootstrap seed (25 seeds per dataset, 10 datasets per condition), by number of iterations, misfit severity, decision rule, item set, and sample size. Lower values of the inter-dimensional correlation mean stronger misfit. Per-condition values carry Monte Carlo standard errors of up to about 3 percentage points and are tabulated in @tbl-stab-appendix.

@fig-stability shows that instability is not monotone in misfit severity or sample size. At $B$ = 2000 the strongest misfit ($\rho$ = .15) left on average `r bb(250)` items per dataset with a seed-dependent flag at $n$ = 250 but `r bb(1000)` at $n$ = 1000, where items were flagged or cleared decisively. Instability arises where the evidence about an item approaches the flagging threshold without clearly passing it, so it is driven by the number of such boundary items rather than by misfit severity or sample size as such. Across the misfit conditions, the probability that two seeds disagreed at $B$ = 2000 ranged from `r sprintf("%.0f", min(dis_cond$pct))` to `r sprintf("%.0f", max(dis_cond$pct))`%. With ten datasets per condition, these results illustrate the dependence rather than giving rates that carry over to other data.

How much instability an analysis shows is thus set by the data. If an item's p-value with unlimited iterations is $\pi$, its Monte Carlo estimate from $B$ iterations has a standard error of about $\sqrt{\pi(1 - \pi)/B}$, so the iterations needed for a reproducible decision grow with the inverse square of the distance between $\pi$ and $\alpha$, and for items close to the threshold no affordable number of iterations removes the instability. Seed sensitivity is therefore a diagnostic. Items whose flags change with the seed are borderline cases that need more data or substantive judgment rather than a luckier seed. The instability of the interval rule at $w$ = .999 declined only slowly with $B$, consistent with its extreme quantiles remaining poorly estimated throughout the practical range.

# Discussion

```{r disc-prep}
#| include: false
# null familywise error of the Westfall-Young rule, dichotomous study
wyq <- function(B_) sprintf("%.1f", null_rules$wy[null_rules$B == B_])

# Westfall-Young null rate from B = 400 by item set, pooled over n
wy_k <- bind_rows(
  null_any |> filter(B >= 400) |> summarise(pct = 100 * mean(wy), .by = B) |>
    mutate(set = "20 dichotomous"),
  bind_part(s_poly, "pval", c("arm", "rep", "k", "n", "rho")) |>
    filter(k == 0, B >= 400) |>
    summarise(any = any(padj_fwer < al5, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(arm, rep, n, B)) |>
    summarise(pct = 100 * mean(any), .by = c(arm, B)) |> rename(set = arm),
  P7 |> filter(k == 0, B >= 400) |>
    summarise(any = any(padj_fwer < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(rep, n, B)) |>
    summarise(pct = 100 * mean(any), .by = B) |> mutate(set = "5 polytomous")
)
wy_k_rng <- sprintf("%.1f and %.1f", min(wy_k$pct), max(wy_k$pct))

# Westfall-Young detection at the anchored misfit level, B = 2000
det_wy <- RP |>
  mutate(is_mis = mapply(function(a, k, it) it %in% mis5(a, k), arm, k, item)) |>
  filter(is_mis, B == 2000)
pc1 <- function(x) sub("\\.0$", "", sprintf("%.1f", x))  # 100.0 prints as 100
dwy <- function(a, n_, k_) pc1(100 * mean(
  det_wy$padj_fwer[det_wy$arm == a & det_wy$n == n_ &
                     det_wy$k == k_] < al5, na.rm = TRUE))
dwyi <- function(a, n_, k_, it) pc1(100 * mean(
  det_wy$padj_fwer[det_wy$arm == a & det_wy$n == n_ & det_wy$k == k_ &
                     det_wy$item == it] < al5, na.rm = TRUE))

# Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg reachability floor at any number of comparisons
bhf   <- function(m_) fmt_n(floor(m_ / 0.05))
```

This paper asked how the interval width and the number of bootstrap iterations should be chosen for simulation-based cutoffs, and whether the interval is the best way to turn a bootstrap into a decision about item fit. The answers are connected. The width is the FWER parameter of the interval rule and is described well by @eq-fwer. The number of iterations required is set by the width, and not by the sample size that the earlier guidance conditioned on. The same bootstrap also supports a p-value rule that targets a chosen error rate directly, detects more misfit at a matched error rate, and needs far fewer iterations.

Detection at the anchored misfit level was modest. With the nine phq9-derived items and a single misfitting item at $\rho$ = .85, the WY rule detected the misfit in `r dwy("phq9", 250, 1)`% of replications at $n$ = 250 and `r dwy("phq9", 150, 1)`% at $n$ = 150, reaching `r dwy("phq9", 1000, 1)`% only at $n$ = 1000, and the interval rule detected less. Two misfitting items were harder to detect than one. When q8 misfit alongside q5, detection of q5 at $n$ = 250 fell from `r dwyi("phq9", 250, 1, 5)`% to `r dwyi("phq9", 250, 2, 5)`%, because items that share a secondary dimension are evaluated against person estimates contaminated by that dimension. At $n$ = 250 or below, an item fit analysis that flags nothing is therefore weak evidence that nothing is wrong, and other methods of evaluating fit should be used alongside it.

One conclusion of Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025] is confirmed and extended. That paper found conditional outfit worse than conditional infit for dichotomous items under the interval rule. Under the WY rule at $B$ = 1000, conditional outfit was calibrated but detected less misfit than infit in every condition studied, for polytomous items as well as dichotomous ones. Its weakness is one of power, and it follows from its larger variability under a true model, which grows with distance from the person mean, so the off-target items that outfit is conventionally recommended for are the ones it handles worst.

## Recommendations for practice

Five recommendations follow from the results.

1. **Decide with the corrected p-value.** Among the decision rules examined, the WY step-down at $\alpha$ = .05 performed best, and it is the recommended decision rule for conditional item fit. Its FWER under the null was at or slightly below the nominal level from $B$ = 400 onward. Holm gave nearly the same results once $B$ cleared its floor of $k/\alpha$ iterations, but the step-down needs no such floor. It also detected more misfit than the interval rule at a matched error rate, and it was the more stable of the two under reseeding. Against BH it holds up even where that procedure is unconstrained: on a five-item scale, whose reachability floor of `r bhf(5)` iterations binds at no $B$ examined here, the two detected the misfitting item equally often while BH flagged roughly half again as many fitting ones. The control holds when all items fit, and once items misfit the false flags on fitting items grow with sample size for every rule, which the fifth recommendation addresses.

2. **Use at least 400 iterations, and more when computation allows.** Below 400 the WY rule was mildly liberal under the null, at `r wyq(100)`% at $B$ = 100, and decisions were noticeably seed-dependent. The probability that two analysts using different seeds disagree about at least one item kept falling past that point, from `r dv["400"]`% at $B$ = 400 to `r dv["2000"]`% at $B$ = 2000, so at least 1000 to 2000 iterations are worth the cost for a final analysis. Neither the sample size nor the number of items sets this requirement. The step-down can reject from $B$ = 1/$\alpha$ = 20 at any scale length, its null rate from $B$ = 400 was between `r wy_k_rng`% across the 5, 9, 15 and 20-item sets with no trend in the number of items, and the floor of 400 is set by calibration and reproducibility. Holm and BH, in contrast, cannot flag even a single standout item below $k/\alpha$ iterations, a floor that grows with the number of items.

3. **Report the interval as a description and set its width to .95.** At w = .95, `r bq(0.95)` iterations bring the interval within 1% of the width it reaches with 10 000, so the band shown to readers covers close to the 95% it claims. At w = .999 the same 1% takes `r bq(0.999)` iterations, far more than is usually run, so the stated width is not the width the reader is actually seeing. A band showing where a fitting item's infit is expected to fall is worth reporting, but only when its stated width is real.

4. **Report the number of iterations and the random seed.** Both are part of the analysis. Without them a reader cannot tell whether a borderline item would have been flagged in a rerun. The seed will however only be useful if the data are also shared.

5. **Remove items one at a time.** This is the workflow recommended by Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025], and its sequential error rates were not evaluated here, since every reported rate refers to a single analysis. It is retained because misfitting items contaminate the total score that the other items are judged against, which is the source of the false flags on fitting items when some items misfit, and removing the most misfitting item first reduces that contamination before the remaining items are judged. Repeated testing across removal rounds adds multiplicity that the corrections studied here do not address, as the Limitations discuss.

Versions of `easyRasch2` before 1.2.0 used $w$ = .999 and $B$ = 250 by default, a setting at which the interval equals the range of the simulated values. From version 1.2.0 the package flags items on the WY p-value, shows the interval at $w$ = .95 and runs 400 iterations by default, and the upcoming version 1.4.1 studentizes the observed and simulated statistics jointly. These recommendations are not confined to users of R. The same analyses are available through `easyRasch2jmv` [@johanssonEasyRasch2jmv2026], a module for the jamovi statistical platform [@jamovi_2026] that delegates every computation to `easyRasch2`, so that results are numerically identical given the same seeds and iteration counts. Simulation-based cutoffs can be more demanding to use than a rule of thumb, since they require a decision about the number of iterations and about which decision rule to apply, and the recommendations given here are meant to make those decisions simpler.

# Limitations

Misfit was induced by two mechanisms only, multidimensionality throughout and random responding in the mechanism check. Other mechanisms, such as local dependence and genuine variation in item discrimination, were not examined.

Each replication is a single pass through the data. No study simulates the iterative workflow in which a flagged item is removed and the remaining items reanalyzed, which is how the procedures are used in practice and the response to their lack of strong control. Its error rates, including the multiplicity added by repeated testing across removal rounds, are the most important open question.

The scope is narrow in further respects. The item sets had 5, 9, 15, and 20 items, so @eq-fwer and the iteration requirements are verified in that range and not for longer instruments. The comparison of conditional infit and outfit was made at one decision rule and iteration count, the WY p-value with $B$ = 1000, and does not necessarily extend to the unconditional outfit that some software reports. Of the FWER procedures only the WY step-down and Holm were compared, and resampling-based false discovery rate procedures [@yekutieliResamplingbasedFalseDiscovery1999] were not included. Benjamini-Hochberg is guaranteed to control the false discovery rate under positive regression dependency [@benjamini_control_2001], but whether that extends to two-sided tests on a residual-based statistic such as conditional infit is open, so its rates here rest on the simulations alone. Joint studentization was evaluated in the dichotomous null conditions only. The two versions differ only in whether the observed value contributes to the moments, a share of 1/($B$ + 1), and in those conditions the difference in familywise error was `r wjd(400)` percentage points at $B$ = 400 and at most `r wjd_max_from(1000)` from $B$ = 1000. A similarly small difference is expected in the polytomous sets and under misfit at the recommended numbers of iterations, but this was not verified. Exact validity at a given sample size, by maximizing the Monte Carlo p-value over the nuisance parameters [@dufour_monte_2006] or, for dichotomous items, by conditioning on the observed margins [@verhelst_efficient_2008], was not examined. Every study used $\alpha$ = .05. The reachability floors and the correspondence between width and familywise error hold at any $\alpha$, but the reported rates and the 400-iteration floor were established at .05, and a smaller $\alpha$ would likely require more iterations. The anchored misfit levels were calibrated against a single instrument with an unusual configuration, two items far above the person mean, and the stylised 15-item set is the only regular configuration it is compared with. Matching on mean infit, finally, does not make different misfit mechanisms equivalent, as the mechanism check shows.

A practical limit appears at the short end. Five polytomous items with four response categories imply fifteen threshold parameters, and at $n$ = 250 `r drop5$n_bad` of the `r fmt_n(drop5$n_all)` bootstraps run in that study produced no usable p-value at all, their simulated statistics having too little variance to studentize by. This did not occur at $n$ = 600 or with 9 items or more, but a five-item scale at a small sample is where the procedure starts to strain.

Large language models were used in preparing this work. The author designed the studies, decided which conditions to run and which results to report, verified the code and the reported values, and is responsible for all content including any errors.

A large language model was used in an agentic coding environment to write and revise the simulation code, to run the studies, and to produce the tables and figures from the cached results. It was also used to draft and revise manuscript text against an outline and instructions specified by the author, and to check the drafted text against the cached results.
